question_text: What causes "shark fin" waveforms on the rising edge of an I2C bus, and what happens if the pull-up resistors are too large?
answer_text: Shark fins occur because the I2C bus relies on passive pull-up resistors to charge the bus capacitance. If the resistor is too large, it takes too long to reach a HIGH state.
explanation_text: I2C is an open-drain protocol, so while devices actively pull the bus LOW very quickly, they rely entirely on the RC time constant (T = R * C) of the pull-up resistor and the parasitic bus capacitance to pull the line HIGH. If the resistor is too large (e.g., 100kΩ instead of 2.2kΩ), the rising edge becomes a slow, curved exponential ramp (a "shark fin"). This can violate timing requirements, causing data corruption.
bonus_question_text: If the pull-up resistors are too small (e.g., 100 ohms), what happens?
bonus_answer_text: It wastes a significant amount of current. Every time a device pulls the line LOW to transmit a 0, it creates a direct path from Vcc to ground through that resistor. A very small resistor means excessive, continuously wasted power while the line is low.
